title: Challenge Accepted: Improving Our Feedback Part 2
author: Zulauf, Ben
summary: Effective instructional feedback requires evaluators to understand how people actually learn, not just check compliance with a rubric. The Simple Model of Teaching -- a six-stage sequential framework (create culture, secure attention, optimize communication, drive thought, gather and give feedback, ensure consolidation) -- provides a diagnostic lens for identifying where learning breaks down and targeting feedback accordingly. The Danielson Framework, while still required for formal ratings, was not designed as a diagnostic tool; evaluators can improve its reliability by adding phrases like "as a result of teacher actions" to clarify instructional causality. Day-to-day feedback should use a framework aligned to how people learn rather than to a compliance-based rubric. The author argues that district administrators have the same obligation to apply learning science to their work with teachers as teachers have to apply it to their work with students. Ultimately, teachers cannot improve if their coaching is focused on demonstrating student-led outcomes rather than developing the intentional teacher moves that produce those outcomes.
points: * The Simple Model of Teaching identifies six sequential fundamental learning problems; evaluators should diagnose which stage is failing before providing feedback. * A rubric that expects students to take initiative at the distinguished level conflates outcomes with teacher actions -- feedback is only useful when it points to what the teacher should do differently. * Consolidation is chronically neglected: learning that appears solid within a lesson often vanishes by the next day because no system exists for revisiting prior material. * Administrators owe teachers the same quality of learning-science-driven practice that teachers owe students -- professional development must be as carefully designed as any lesson. * Steplab's Simple Model offers an alternative to Danielson for day-to-day coaching, because it is built around how people learn rather than around observable student-initiative milestones.
quotes: If a teacher asks a diagnostic question with very targeted distractors and then bases her next instructional move on students' responses, that's a distinguished characteristic.
Students need to be able to anticipate classroom structures so that they are better able to attend to the information that's presented.
The care and attention to detail that we want teachers to put into planning for students is exactly what I should be putting into the work I do with teachers and administrators.
If we want to increase consistency in instructional feedback, then we need to provide a tool that helps us arrive at the same starting point.
